drills.q: Prove that greedy policy improvement never makes any state's value worse.
drills.a: By construction Q^pi(s,pi'(s)) >= Q^pi(s,pi(s)) = V^pi(s). Chain this forward: substitute the same inequality at each future timestep (V^pi(s_t+k) <= Q^pi(s_t+k, pi'(s_t+k)) again and again), producing V^pi(s) <= ... <= V^pi'(s). The inequality direction is preserved at every substitution so it holds in the limit.

drills.q: A policy iteration loop never terminates in your implementation. Name the top three things to check, tied to the actual convergence proof.
drills.a: 1) Policy-equality check uses exact per-state action match, not float comparison, with deterministic tie-breaking in argmax. 2) gamma < 1, required for the evaluation contraction. 3) P(s'|s,a) sums to 1 for every (s,a), required for the improvement monotonicity proof.

drills.q: Why is policy iteration's termination argument fundamentally different from value iteration's convergence argument?
drills.a: Policy iteration's argument is combinatorial: finitely many deterministic policies, each iteration strictly improves or stops, so it must terminate -- it gives no rate guarantee. Value iteration's argument is analytic: the Bellman optimality operator is a contraction on a continuous space of value functions (Banach fixed point), which gives a geometric rate gamma^n.

drills.q: A team has a fully-known MDP with 3000 states and wants to train a DQN on it instead of running value iteration. Evaluate this decision.
drills.a: Usually wrong: with a known model and enumerable states, tabular value/policy iteration gives the exact optimum in milliseconds with zero sampling noise or function-approximation error, while DQN adds all of those risks to solve a problem that doesn't need them. Only justified if the model changes frequently or this is deliberately a stepping stone to a much larger version of the problem.

drills.q: Your state space is a 10^9-cell grid with local transitions (each cell reaches ~4 neighbors). Can tabular DP still work, and what modification would you reach for first?
drills.a: Per-sweep cost becomes roughly linear in |S| with sparse transitions, so a sweep is plausible, but storing V over 10^9 states and the sweep count to converge remain issues. Reach for asynchronous DP / prioritized sweeping to focus computation on states with large pending Bellman error rather than uniformly sweeping everything.

drills.q: You extract a policy from V before value iteration has converged. What's wrong with this, precisely?
drills.a: The policy is greedy w.r.t. an intermediate, still-wrong value estimate, with no principled optimality guarantee. The value-error-to-policy-suboptimality bound is 2*gamma*eps/(1-gamma), so an unconverged V (large eps) can produce a policy far from optimal, especially as gamma approaches 1.
